chunks: Why protect against over/undervoltage and overcurrent. The question: How/why do you want to protect against overcurrent and/or over/undervoltage conditions?
Every part has limits, and real systems regularly go beyond them. Too much current heats wires and parts, because heat grows with the square of the current.
Too much voltage punches through the thin insulating layers inside parts. Too little voltage makes logic misbehave and transistors run half on.
Protection is whatever stops those things: a fuse, a clamp, or a supervisor chip that holds the system in reset while the supply is low.
You stack several layers so one failure does not destroy everything.
Think of a house. The circuit breaker is the overcurrent protection: it cuts power before the wires overheat.
A surge protector is the overvoltage protection: it absorbs a spike from a lightning strike.
And when the lights dim and the fridge stutters during a brownout, that is the undervoltage problem. Nothing burns, but equipment behaves strangely.
The analogy leaves out one thing: in a circuit board the protection parts are tiny, so they must be chosen for the energy of the fault.
Heating rises faster than I squared (the exponent is 1 over 0. 44 about 2. 27 ).
Doubling the current from 1 amps to 2 amps raises this trace from about 13 degrees Celsius to about 64 degrees Celsius above ambient.
A short circuit doesn't just run hotter, it leaves the safe region entirely.
Drag the width to 20 mil: the same 2 amps now heats it by only about 20 degrees Celsius, because cross-section enters with an exponent of 0. 725.
Joule heating: heat from current in a resistance, P equals I squared R . Absolute maximum rating: the limit past which a part may be damaged.
TVS diode: a clamp that absorbs short, high-energy voltage spikes. UVLO (undervoltage lockout): holding a circuit off until the supply is high enough.
Brown-out: a supply sag below the operating minimum, but not to zero.
Short a 5 volts rail through 10 milliohms. The ideal current would be 5 over 0. 01 equals 500 amps, which would dissipate 500 squared times 0. 01 equals 2.
5 kilowatts in a few millimeters of copper. A real supply cannot deliver that, but even a few amps can burn a thin trace. Doubling any current quadruples the heating.
Now the other end: a microcontroller rail that sags below its minimum may run garbage or half-write its saved settings, with no smoke at all. That is the whole idea.
"Every component has limits, and real systems leave the nominal range: shorts, hot-plug spikes, wrong adapters, sagging batteries.
Overcurrent is a heating problem since power goes as I squared R. Overvoltage causes breakdown of oxides and capacitors. Undervoltage makes logic misbehave and FETs run half on.
So I layer protection: a fuse or eFuse and TVS at the input, current limit and thermal shutdown in the regulator, and a supervisor or UVLO so the system only runs when the rails are healthy."
Quick check. Why is overcurrent so damaging compared with a modest voltage increase in a conductor?
